back: Timber from deciduous trees that lose their leaves in autumn. Slow-growing, so less available and more expensive.
Timber from evergreen coniferous trees with cones and needles. Faster-growing, readily available and cheaper.
Hardwood; moderate brown with close, straight grain. Tough, durable and polishes well — high-quality furniture, doors and staircases.
Hardwood; pink-tinted and closely grained. Very tough with a smooth finish — workbenches and hard-wearing products.
Hardwood; dark red-brown, very close grain. Cuts and polishes easily — furniture and cabinet making.
A fast-growing hardwood that is soft and very lightweight — used for modelling.
Hardwood; pale, fine grain, easy to work and lightweight — used for modelling and pattern making.
Softwood; pale yellow with darker brown grain, lightweight and easy to work — construction and furniture.
Softwood; lightweight, pale and even-textured, good outdoors — fencing, decking and sheds.
Softwood; darker with brown grain, water resistant and durable — exterior cladding and boats.
Softwood; pale, fine grain, almost knot-free and hard for a softwood — interior joinery and stairs.
Kiln drying or air drying natural timber to remove moisture and prevent shrinkage before use.
Man-made boards made from wood fibres (usually recycled) bonded with resins into sheets.
Small fibres mixed with wax and resin, heated and compressed. No grain, easy to work but very porous — seal edges before finishing.
Small chips of timber bonded together into a dense sheet. Usually veneered or given a melamine layer, e.g. kitchen worktops.
Layers of wood bonded with grain at 90° to each other — strong and rigid; used for furniture and construction.
Compressed wood fibres with one smooth face; thin and hard — back panels and drawer bases.

front: Standard sheet size of manufactured boards
back: 2440 mm × 1220 mm, or a half sheet of 1220 mm × 610 mm.
